Work.title: Work
Work.description: Six projects, six different contexts. The focus here isn't the numbers — it's the reasoning: what the problem was, how I understood it, what I decided to drop and why.

amadeus.title: Unifying data products through a new transformation platform
amadeus.summary: Leading a new product for dataset transformation and management, part of a company-wide push to unify Amadeus's data-oriented products.
amadeus.context: Amadeus runs several data-oriented products that grew independently of each other. Leadership decided to unify them under a shared strategy, which means this product has to fit into a much larger technical and organizational picture from day one.
amadeus.role: Senior Product Manager owning the new dataset transformation and management product, working closely with partnership teams to turn client needs into concrete requirements.
amadeus.discovery: Still early days in this role. Most of the work so far has been mapping how client and partner needs translate into what the product actually needs to cover, and understanding how it fits alongside the other data products in the unification effort.
amadeus.decisionFramework: Prioritizing partner input over internal assumptions, and using AI tools daily — Claude, Cursor — to prototype and validate direction quickly before committing engineering time to it.
amadeus.whatIBuilt: Early prototypes and workflow automations, built hands-on with Claude and Cursor, used to test ideas with partners before writing formal specs.
amadeus.outcomes: Too early to share outcomes — this is an active, ongoing role. I'll update this case study as the product matures.

fourvenues.title: Launching a new vertical SaaS product from scratch
fourvenues.summary: Leading the 0→1 of a vertical SaaS product, from the first discovery conversation to production.
fourvenues.context: Fourvenues spotted an opportunity within its vertical that no existing product covered well. There was no product yet, just a business hypothesis and a fast-moving market. The challenge wasn't building fast — it was building the right thing without an internal data history to lean on.
fourvenues.role: Product Manager leading the 0→1: from framing the problem to prioritizing the roadmap and coordinating day to day with design, engineering and the commercial team.
fourvenues.discovery: Interviews with current clients and prospects, shadowing sales calls to understand real objections, and analyzing how users were solving the problem today with improvised tools (spreadsheets, manual processes). The goal was to find the job people were already trying to do, not invent a new one.
fourvenues.decisionFramework: I prioritized on two axes: how often the pain showed up and the cost of not solving it. I dropped features that sounded good on a call but that no client asked for twice. Every line on the roadmap had to answer one question: what business decision does this unlock that can't be made today?
fourvenues.whatIBuilt: The initial product roadmap, the core flows of the first version, and a continuous discovery system with the commercial team so customer feedback reached product without friction.
fourvenues.outcomes: No exact metrics to share yet — the product is still early. Main lesson: in 0→1, the most valuable roadmap is the one that's brave enough to leave things out. Saying no early saves months later.

nailted.title: Redesigning onboarding and lifting weekly engagement
nailted.summary: Redesigned the onboarding flow and the weekly engagement cycle so teams would adopt the product beyond week one.
nailted.context: The product sold well, but real adoption within each team — weekly usage, not just the first login — was uneven. Some teams turned it into a habit; others dropped it once the novelty wore off.
nailted.role: Owned onboarding and engagement: research, flow design, and coordination with design and engineering on the redesign.
nailted.discovery: In-product behavioral analysis to see where people dropped off, combined with interviews with HR managers (the buyers) and employees (the actual users) — because in B2B2C the person who buys and the person who uses it don't always want the same thing.
nailted.decisionFramework: I prioritized changes that shrank the gap between 'I signed up' and 'I understand why this matters every week', over adding new functionality. I dropped visual redesigns that didn't attack the real cause of churn.
nailted.whatIBuilt: A step-by-step onboarding tailored to the role (HR manager vs. employee) and a redesign of the weekly cycle so the interaction felt like part of the team's rhythm, not one more task.
nailted.outcomes: Observable improvement in weekly adoption, no exact figure I can share. Key lesson: in B2B2C you have to design for two audiences with different motivations at once — solving for one doesn't mean you've solved for the other.

cuatroochenta.title: Managing multiple product lines in a consultancy environment
cuatroochenta.summary: Led several tailor-made product lines for different clients at once, each with its own context and constraints.
cuatroochenta.context: A consultancy environment: every client brought their own problem, their own stakeholder and their own definition of success. There wasn't a single product to optimize — there were several running in parallel, each competing for the same team.
cuatroochenta.role: Led full product lifecycle for several accounts at the same time.
cuatroochenta.discovery: Discovery adapted to each client — in consultancy there's no single process that fits everyone. It was about quickly figuring out what information was signal and what was noise in each new context.
cuatroochenta.decisionFramework: I prioritized across product lines with the same criterion every time: real impact on the client's business versus the opportunity cost of the shared team. I dropped requests that solved a one-off symptom for a client without fitting the rest of the portfolio.
cuatroochenta.whatIBuilt: Prioritization systems and processes that let the same squad serve several clients without losing focus, and tailor-made roadmaps fitted to each contract.
cuatroochenta.outcomes: No exact metrics per client. Main lesson: managing product in consultancy is as much about managing expectations as managing a backlog — the trade-off isn't just what to build, it's who to say no to this week.

kokoro-kids.title: Running Scrum for a small edtech team in a fast-changing market
kokoro-kids.summary: Managed sprint planning and roadmap phases for a small, highly competent team adapting an edtech product to a demanding early-stage market.
kokoro-kids.context: Kokoro Kids operated in a young, fast-moving edtech market where user needs and competitive pressure shifted quickly. The team was small and skilled, but needed a clear planning rhythm to keep shipping without losing direction.
kokoro-kids.role: Product Manager responsible for project planning: running Scrum, organizing sprints and tasks, and shaping upcoming product phases.
kokoro-kids.discovery: Close, constant contact with a small team meant discovery happened mostly through daily conversations and fast iteration rather than formal research — the team could test an idea and get a read on it within days.
kokoro-kids.decisionFramework: I prioritized whatever kept the product credible in a market that could shift under us quickly, over polishing features nobody outside the team was asking for yet.
kokoro-kids.whatIBuilt: A predictable sprint cadence and a rolling plan for upcoming phases, giving a small team enough structure to move fast without constant re-planning.
kokoro-kids.outcomes: No exact metrics from this period. Main lesson: in a small, capable team, the PM's job is less about controlling process and more about protecting focus.

playjoy.title: A multiplayer traditional-games app with community at its core
playjoy.summary: A B2C product for traditional games, built to be played in groups, with community as the growth engine.
playjoy.context: Traditional games (cards, board, playground) have an advantage most digital games don't: a community that already plays them offline. The challenge was bringing that social dynamic into a digital product without losing what made it fun.
playjoy.role: Product Manager for the B2C product, focused on multiplayer and community dynamics.
playjoy.discovery: Direct observation of how people play these games offline — who invites, who organizes, what makes a group come back to play the following week.
playjoy.decisionFramework: I prioritized features that reinforced the network effect (inviting, replaying with the same group) over adding more games to the catalog. I dropped functionality that optimized for the individual player instead of the group.
playjoy.whatIBuilt: Cross-platform flows to create and join group games, designed so that organizing a match was as easy as proposing it in a chat.
playjoy.outcomes: No exact figures to share. Lesson: in a product with network effects, the user who really matters isn't the one playing — it's the one organizing. Designing for the organizer multiplies reach.

Community.framing: Built Valencia's most active product community from zero — because I believed the community already existed, it just needed a real place to meet.
Community.story: Carlos founded Valencia Product Beers to test a simple hypothesis: that a product community already existed in Valencia that genuinely wanted to meet and share — tired of events where someone's always selling something. The goal was to move LinkedIn connections into real ones. Beer is just the icebreaker. It's not his first community, either — before this he co-organized FreemoteHouse, Reset Weekend and NOSOLOENLARED, building spaces for founders and remote workers to actually meet each other.

About.bio1: Senior Technical Product Manager with 5+ years building and scaling B2B and B2C SaaS products in integration-heavy, partner-facing environments. I lead API-based integrations end to end — translating technical and business requirements into clear specs, then orchestrating engineering, data, operations and external partners to ship them.
About.bio2: I'm a daily user of AI tooling — Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot — to prototype, debug and ship automations myself, not just write specs and hand them off. Discovery is not a phase, it's a habit, and the best roadmap is the one that kills the most bad ideas early.
About.bio3: Outside work, I run Valencia Product Beers — a community I built because I was tired of fake networking events. We meet, we talk product, we drink beer. Simple.
